item.title: From Radio Waves to CSI: The Physics of WiFi Channel Measurement
item.description: The two WiFi-sensing posts in this series — ESPectre and RuView — both treat CSI as a given: the chip hands it out, the algorithm consumes it, everyone is happy. But where does CSI itself come from? Why does a physical layer designed to move data incidentally measure the whole room? This post digs out the foundation, written for two kinds of readers: if you are new to WiFi sensing, read from the top — every section starts from intuition and closes with the formula; if you have already played with ESPectre, jump straight to the second half — traffic sources, range, and capability boundaries, the shared physical ledger behind all three posts.

item.title: Turn an ESP32 into a WiFi Motion Sensor: ESPectre Principles and Deployment
item.description: If you want to know whether someone is moving in a room, the two off-the-shelf options are both awkward. Cameras raise privacy problems and are off-limits in bedrooms and bathrooms. PIR sensors rely on infrared, fail behind a glass cabinet, and false-trigger on air-conditioning drafts. ESPectre takes a different angle: the room is already full of WiFi signals, and human movement disturbs them — so just read the change in the signal. It turns a ten-dollar ESP32 into a motion sensor with no camera, no microphone, and no dedicated mmWave radar; the router is the one you already own.

item.title: RuView: WiFi-Based Pose Estimation and Contactless Vital Signs
item.description:
The previous post covered ESPectre, which uses WiFi CSI to answer “is anyone moving in the room?” RuView wants more: not just motion, but 17 body keypoints, breathing rate, heart rate, and through-wall sensing, all decoded from the same signals. It is written in Rust by ruvnet (the author of claude-flow), MIT-licensed, and with 92,000+ stars as of September 2026 it is the hottest open-source project in this space.

The conclusion first, so you don’t over-expect: this is a beta-stage research platform. The gap between the pose model’s benchmark-dataset score and its on-device score is large, and APIs and firmware are still moving. It still deserves a serious write-up for two reasons. First, the pipeline is a textbook-grade WiFi-sensing architecture — from multi-band fusion to vital-sign extraction, every stage carries something transferable to other sensing problems. Second, the project labels “which numbers are real and which are scaffolding” in an explicit three-tier maturity table — that level of honest self-labeling is rare in open-source AI projects.
